29048-the-fabric-of-civilization-a-short:
The Guaranty Trust Company of New York published this 1919 survey, The Fabric of Civilization, on the cotton industry in the United States. The survey aims to give general facts in brief compass, not to cover every corner of the field, so a reader can quickly learn the industry's broader outlines. A cotton price chart, showing spot prices for middling uplands in New York, fronts the book.

Chapters treat the importance and power of cotton, where it is grown and spun, the raw cotton market, the cloth market, and financing. Later chapters cover American cloth abroad, the grower's problems, the mill, and finishing operations. Readers get a banker's clear survey of an industry that touched most lives on earth, built peoples, and sometimes tore them apart.
31891-essays-on-the-constitution-of-the-:
Paul Leicester Ford's 1892 collection Essays on the Constitution of the United States, published during its discussion by the people in 1787 and 1788, gathers the pamphlet arguments of ratification. Ford had earlier selected fourteen tracts for his Pamphlets on the Constitution, and this volume extends that work.

Its contents include the letters of Cassius by James Sullivan, Agrippa accredited to James Winthrop. They also include the Landholder letters of Oliver Ellsworth, Cato by George Clinton, Caesar by Alexander Hamilton, Sydney by Robert Yates, and a letter of caution by Samuel Chase. Readers get the ratification debate in the voices of its participants, Federalist and Anti-Federalist alike.
34123-familiar-letters-of-john-adams-and:
Charles Francis Adams's 1876 volume gathers familiar letters of John Adams and his wife Abigail Adams, written during the Revolution. Adams adds a memoir of Mrs. Adams, and draws on two earlier selections, the first of which ran through four editions in eight years.

The letters run between husband and wife through the years of the struggle, mixing public news with home cares, money, health, and hope. Readers meet the Revolution as a family lived it, in voices that are frank, fond, and often tired, across a long and hard war. Adams notes that the first series pleased the public, while the second sold more slowly, till both ran out.
7176-a-letter-to-a-hindu:
Leo Tolstoy wrote this letter in Russian in reply to the editor of Free Hindustan, and M. K. Gandhi's introduction tells how it passed from hand to hand before it reached him. Gandhi saw its worth at once, translated it into Gujarati, urged versions in other Indian tongues, and then had Tolstoy confirm the typed copy and grant leave to print it. The letter bears the subtitle The Subjection of India, Its Cause and Cure.

Tolstoy speaks straight to an Indian reader about rule from abroad and the path out of it, in the plain moral voice of his later years. Gandhi's framing makes the letter a bridge between a Russian prophet and an Indian cause, short in length but wide in aim. The volume preserves both the letter and the story of its journey into print.
a-letter-to-a-hindu:
Leo Tolstoy wrote A Letter to a Hindu as a reply to the editor of the journal Free Hindustan, and the hosted edition carries an introduction by M. K. Gandhi, who championed the letter in India. Its subtitle states the theme plainly: the subjection of India, its cause and its cure. Tolstoy, an old soldier turned Christian thinker, addresses Indians who hoped to end British rule.

He argues that India was not conquered by English strength so much as surrendered by Indian cooperation with violence, commerce, and military service. Against assassination and armed revolt he sets the law of love and non-resistance to evil, borne through self-suffering. Gandhi's introduction explains why he thought the letter worth translating and spreading, and it became a seed text for nonviolent resistance.

france-parlement-aix-en-provence-france-: Arrest du Parlement du Provence, du premier mars 1755. The Provençal decree. This book preserves that arrest. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
nasa-tm-19650020354-apollo-usb-system-mu:
B Kruger at Goddard wrote this report on April 21, 1965, about a problem in the Apollo communication system. The system was the USB, or Unified S-Band, link. It carried many signals at once by phase modulation on one carrier. Mixing many signals that way can distort each of them.

Kruger lays out the multisignal phase modulation problems and their solutions. A spectrum analysis of the carrier lies behind the work, the catalog note says. Apollo crews would depend on that single link for voice, data, and ranging. Sorting out its distortion problems on paper, years before flight, was essential ground work.
nasa-tm-19700018977-configuration-of-the:
D. H. Fairfield and N. F. Ness of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in May 1970. It studies the shape of Earth's magnetic tail during substorms. The tail is the long stretch of Earth's field blown away from the Sun, and substorms are sudden bursts of activity in that region.

The authors extend earlier comparisons between tail measurements and ground records from the auroral zone. Those comparisons had hinted that the tail's shape changes sharply during a substorm. Fairfield and Ness use vector field readings from the IMP 4 spacecraft to test that link. They then discuss what the changes mean for the many substorm effects seen on the ground and in space.
nasa-tm-19700027268-equatorial-scintilla:
NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center issued this preprint in June 1970. It reports radio scintillations near the equator that were met during support of the Apollo 13 mission. The events were logged from March 30 to April 18, 1970. Scintillation is a rapid fading and flutter of a radio signal passing through disturbed upper air.

The records come through the ATS 1 satellite link watched from ground stations during the flight. Signal level charts track the link day by day at Mojave, Rosman, and Iwo Jima. A cumulative chart gathers how the signal levels spread across the whole period. Conclusions and recommendations close the report, with one earlier record from Lima, Peru, kept for comparison.
podcast-dannyjones-t9Xsj_7ULDU:
YouTube prank star Jack Tenney of Joogsquad joins Danny Jones for KONCRETE number 6. Forest gives him a grand intro as a world-renowned wild man. Tenney is also brother to famed gamer Tfue.

The group jokes that Tenney serves as his dad's conscience and nemesis. Talk covers pranks, family fame, and life on camera. Tenney explains how stunts built a huge young audience. podcast-joerogan-XMK1KEk5OdU:
Defector Yeonmi Park tells Rogan, in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, about escaping North Korea. Park fled as a teenager across a frozen river into China, then faced years of danger before reaching the free world. Her memoir made her one of the best-known defectors alive.

She describes hunger under the regime, the fear that governed daily life, and what freedom felt like once she reached it. Rogan asks about the parts of her story that draw attacks and doubt. The segment is a gripping first-hand account of a closed country, told by someone who paid full price to leave it.
